name: Obadiah
interpretive_note: This entry's reference list appears to bundle two men roughly two and a half centuries apart: an official named Obadiah whom King Jehoshaphat sent to teach the Law throughout Judah (2 Chronicles 17:7, 9th century BC), and a Levite gatekeeper named Obadiah, also called Abda, descended from Jeduthun, who lived in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:16; Nehemiah 11:17, 5th century BC). Scripture records no independent action for the later gatekeeper beyond his place in a residency list, so this entry's narrative content is drawn from Jehoshaphat's teaching mission; the two references most likely describe different individuals who share a name rather than one person.
source_summary: One of five officials King Jehoshaphat sent throughout Judah to teach the Book of the Law among the people; a different, much later Obadiah (also called Abda) appears only as a name in post-exilic Levite gatekeeper lists.
family_friendly_summary: Obadiah was one of five officials King Jehoshaphat chose for an important job. Jehoshaphat wanted everyone in Judah to know God's law, so early in his reign he sent Obadiah and four other officials, along with priests and Levites, to travel through every town in Judah teaching the people from the Book of the Law. It was a coordinated, kingdom-wide effort to help God's people actually know what He had commanded them. Jehoshaphat was one of Judah's better kings, and this teaching mission was part of the bigger story of his effort to lead the nation back to faithfully following God.
adult_story: Obadiah is named among five officials -- Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah -- whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent throughout the kingdom in the third year of his reign as part of an organized program of religious instruction (2 Chronicles 17:7). Jehoshaphat paired these officials with a team of Levites and two priests, Elishama and Jehoram (17:8), and together "they taught in Judah, having the book of the law of the LORD with them; and they went throughout all the cities of Judah and taught among the people" (17:9). This was a deliberate, circuit-style teaching campaign reaching the whole of Judah, part of the broader reforms Chronicles credits to Jehoshaphat, including removing pagan high places and Asherim (17:6). The chapter connects this teaching mission to the kingdom's resulting stability: surrounding nations, in awe of the LORD's hand on Judah, brought tribute rather than making war (17:10-11). Scripture gives Obadiah no further individual action beyond his place on this team. A different, much later Obadiah -- also called Abda, son of Shammua and descended from Jeduthun -- appears only as a name in genealogical lists of Levite gatekeepers who resettled Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:16; Nehemiah 11:17), with no narrative of his own; the two men are best read as separate individuals who happen to share a name.
